clue.text: Scientific fact maybe lacking substance — flat-earthers most stupid

indicators.note: a stupid arrangement is a muddled one, so these letters are jumbled
with no substance inside, the word maybe keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: only its first and last letters survive
taken as written for the anagram pool

explanation.surface: A jibe that flat-earthers, the dimmest of all, reject even the most solid scientific facts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scientific fact maybe' looks like one definition phrase, but 'maybe' belongs to the wordplay: emptied of its middle it leaves two letters for the pool.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous result of Pierre de Fermat, finally proved by Andrew Wiles, is an established mathematical truth.

clue.text: Foreign land line scary: phone mobile connected with female

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all telephones — line, phone, mobile — and not one word of it suggests the South Pacific. That distance between surface and answer is what makes a long anagram hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: This overseas collectivity of South Pacific islands, Tahiti among them, is a territory abroad for a British solver: a definition by example.

clue.text: Once more broadcast concerning series

parts.note: re = concerning, as in memo headers
a run = a series (of shows, results…)

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a line from a television listing, which is how the definition and the wordplay manage to hide inside the same sentence about repeats.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to screen a programme again, and its past participle is unchanged, so it stands in for the phrase as a plain synonym.

clue.text: Host, part of TV duo, is a crawler

explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' is placed to look like a presenter standing beside his co-star, and it means a multitude instead. ANT is worth knowing in its own right — the crossword's standard worker.
explanation.definitionFit: These tropical insects march in huge foraging columns across the forest floor, so they are one kind of creeping creature: a definition by example.

clue.text: Club foot out of sock that is tiny without padding

parts.note: TINY with no 'padding' (inner letters) leaves T…Y

explanation.walkthrough: Two deletions dressed up as clothing: the foot comes off a sock, and the padding is the soft middle of a word. Both sit so neatly in the surface that neither reads as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name an organised association of members sharing an interest, such as a debating or golfing one, so this is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Order at local store, ultimately to get deal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' opens the clue looking like something you place at a shop counter, and it is the anagram instruction. Indicators like the first word, where they pass as ordinary nouns.
explanation.definitionFit: To deal is to hand out shares, as a dealer does with cards, and the answer means to assign portions: a plain synonym in the verb sense.

clue.text: Act in theatre work: PG film essentially getting released

indicators.note: letters that are released are set free from their order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram pool
taken as written, the film certificate letters

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its centre, so only the middle letters of film are used

parts.note: its middle two letters are kept

explanation.surface: A note that a stage production, a PG-rated film at heart, is being released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' reads as part of the theatre picture, but it means a performer's turn, as in a circus act.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone balancing high on a wire is a classic circus or variety performance, a turn on the bill.

clue.text: Squash flies all over the place with end of swat

explanation.walkthrough: Every word belongs to one picture of swatting flies, so nothing sticks out as fodder or as instruction. That is what a well-made anagram looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: To squash a protest or a yawn is to suppress it, and the answer carries the same sense of smothering: a plain synonym in the verb sense.

clue.text: Small place cleared to screen one sad film

parts.note: PLACE 'cleared' of its middle leaves P…E

explanation.walkthrough: 'To screen' does both jobs at once: it is the container instruction, meaning to conceal, and it belongs to the world of the answer. WEE for small is Scots, and a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British name for a tear-jerking movie or novel, coined from the crying it is designed to provoke in its audience.

clue.text: See 1
Pass person inhaling good scent

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is someone walking past and catching a whiff, which is why 'Pass' reads as a verb. It is a noun here — a col, the dip between two peaks.
explanation.definitionFit: Eau de toilette named after the German city where it was first made is a light perfume, so a plain synonym for a fragrance.

clue.text: Withdraw sheath for contraceptive during enjoyable time to get pregnant

indicators.note: placed during the outing means put inside it

parts.note: an enjoyable time out with someone is a fun date

indicators.note: withdrawing pulls something back, so the two letters are taken in reverse order
a sheath is the outer covering, so only the outside letters of the next word are taken

parts.note: its first and last letters form the sheath

explanation.surface: Smutty advice on removing a condom mid-date in order to conceive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheath for contraceptive' reads as a condom, but the sheath is just the outer letters of the word contraceptive.
explanation.definitionFit: To fecundate is to make fertile or impregnate, i.e. to cause a female to get pregnant.

clue.text: Focus for rescuing sheep in distress

explanation.walkthrough: 'Focus for' is an unusual way of asking for the exact middle of a word. And the definition is idiom rather than dictionary: you are cut up when something has upset you.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial idiom, chiefly British, for being upset or grief-stricken, used after 'feel' or 'be' just as the definition is.

clue.text: Sexpot stripped for show

indicators.note: stripped of its outer covering, the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: the word whose inside letters are kept

explanation.surface: An alluring person undressing as part of a performance.
explanation.definitionFit: An expo is a large public exhibition, a trade or industry show.

clue.text: Intimate squeezing partner's core, relaxed in armchair?

indicators.note: one word squeezes another by holding it inside

parts.note: to intimate is to hint or say indirectly

indicators.note: the core of a word is its central letter, here the middle of partner

parts.note: relaxed and comfortable means at home

explanation.surface: Two lovers cuddling up, the pair snug and relaxed together in an armchair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intimate' looks like an adjective about lovers; it is the verb meaning to suggest.
explanation.definitionFit: An armchair traveller or critic is one who stays put rather than going out, so the adjective means homebound.

clue.text: I squeeze into casual suit that could be taken in when not satisfied?

definitions.text: that could be taken in when not satisfied?

indicators.note: the two pieces go into the rearranged word
a casual arrangement is a loose, haphazard one, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: to squeeze in is to ram, cram

explanation.surface: Someone forcing themselves into a relaxed suit that needs altering, taken in if it doesn't fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' suggests tailoring a suit; in the definition it means eaten, as a dessert when still hungry.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian coffee-flavoured pudding is something eaten at the end of a meal if one is still hungry.

clue.text: Destroying climate, sun reaches highest point

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a headline about the sun destroying the climate, topical enough that you read it for meaning and never count the letters sitting in front of you.
explanation.definitionFit: In astronomy a star does this when it crosses the meridian at its highest altitude, and figuratively anything climaxing does too: a plain synonym.

clue.text: Apple device set up date feature on smartphone

parts.note: the computer; 'set up' reverses it in a down clue
a date = an era, a period

explanation.walkthrough: The tech surface never once mentions photography, and 'set up' is positional: in a down clue it lifts MAC back up the grid rather than telling you to arrange anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Almost every mobile phone carries a built-in lens for taking photographs, so this is a definition by example.

clue.text: Rescue from island — lifeboat team wanting number in back of boat

parts.note: aft = the back of a boat

explanation.walkthrough: A maritime surface hiding an answer that happens by air. The RNLI is the sort of British initialism worth having ready — setters reach for it whenever a clue goes near the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: An evacuation by aircraft, typically of people stranded by disaster or injury, is one kind of saving: a definition by example.

clue.text: Give authority? Those people might

explanation.walkthrough: The second half of the clue winks at its own answer: those people might, indeed, em-power. And 'EM for them is apostrophe-dropped speech, a favourite two-letter piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant someone official or legal power to act is a plain synonym; the question mark nods to the self-referential second half.

clue.text: Risk money accepting a flutter

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is a straight swap: 'flutter' looks like the betting word and 'risk money' like the definition, when it is the other way round. A flutter is what a heart does.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart's flutter is a pulse or throb, so a plain synonym in the noun sense of a single rhythmic stroke.

clue.text: Stylish attempt to cover butt

explanation.walkthrough: 'Butt' is a cigarette end, not the anatomy the surface invites you to picture. Hearing 'attempt' as a noun is the other small step.
explanation.definitionFit: Fashionable and up to date, an informal plain synonym describing clothes, places or people in vogue.

clue.text: Form of comic, Mark, with one short joke

explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised, Mark looks like a man being addressed; it is the old German currency, and M is its abbreviation. Setters dress abbreviations as proper names constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Japanese comic books and graphic novels make up a distinctive genre with its own drawing style, so a definition by example.

clue.text: Rake with money returned to pick up sex worker

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rake' is the trap: not the garden tool but the eighteenth-century wastrel, a sense you meet far more often in crosswords than in life.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned word for a dissolute, immoral man, and an unprincipled scoundrel is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Visible hole on green

explanation.walkthrough: The golfing surface, hole and green, is entirely decorative. VERT is heraldry's green, and it sits alongside OR for gold as a colour a setter can turn into letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Done openly and not concealed, a plain synonym; it is the opposite of covert.

clue.text: He scored from ball into box, missing header during international

parts.note: in football, a ball into the penalty box is a cross
CROSS loses its first letter — a football pun on 'header'

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as football and is really about opera, with 'missing header' the best pun in the puzzle: a header removed means the first letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian composer of The Barber of Seville wrote musical scores, so he is defined by what he did, with 'scored' in its musical sense.

clue.text: Drunk with wine drinking fizzy stuff out of round

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an ordinary evening's drinking, and the two smallest words do the most work — 'with' is a single letter, and 'round' is the O taken out of the coke.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for very intoxicated, from the image of being ruined or smashed, so a plain synonym.

clue.text: Polluter to run after dirty river checked by Environment Agency

parts.note: adult = dirty, as in adult movies
its initials, wrapped round the R: E(R)A
TO + R (r = run, as on a cricket scorecard)

explanation.walkthrough: A dirty river being checked by the Environment Agency is a complete and plausible news story, which is the red herring. 'Dirty' for adult, as in adult films, is the piece to see first.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes food or drink impure by adding inferior substances contaminates it, so a plain synonym.
